In [[probability theory]], a '''superprocess''' is a measure-valued [[stochastic process]] that is usually constructed as a special limit of near-critical branching diffusions.

Informally, a superprocess can be seen as a branching process where each particle splits and dies at infinite rates, and evolves in a state space {{mvar|E}} according to a diffusion equation. We follow the rescaled population of particles, seen as a measure on {{mvar|E}}.

== Scaling limit of a discrete branching process ==

=== Simplest setting ===
[[File:Branching Brownian process..svg|thumb|Branching Brownian process for N=30]]
For any integer <math>N\geq 1</math>, consider a branching Brownian process <math>Y^N(t,dx)</math> defined as follows:

* Start at <math>t=0</math> with <math>N</math> independent particles distributed according to a probability distribution <math>\mu</math>.
* Each particle independently move according to a [[Brownian motion]].
* Each particle independently dies with rate <math>N</math>.
* When a particle dies, with probability <math>1/2</math> it gives birth to two offspring in the same location.

The notation <math>Y^N(t,dx)</math> means should be interpreted as: at each time <math>t</math>, the number of particles in a set <math>A\subset \mathbb{R}</math> is <math>Y^N(t,A)</math>. In other words, <math>Y</math> is a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]]-valued random process.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last=Li |first=Zenghu |chapter=Measure-Valued Branching Processes |date=2011 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-15004-3_2 |title=Measure-Valued Branching Markov Processes |series=Probability and Its Applications |pages=29–56 |editor-last=Li |editor-first=Zenghu |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-15004-3_2 |isbn=978-3-642-15004-3 |access-date=2022-12-20|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Now, define a rescaled process:

<math>X^N(t,dx):=\frac{1}{N}Y^N(t,dx)</math>

Then the finite-dimensional distributions of <math>X^N</math> converge as <math>N\to +\infty</math> to those of a measure-valued random process <math>X(t,dx)</math>, which is called a <math>(\xi,\phi)</math>-'''''superprocess''''',<ref name=":0" /> with initial value <math>X(0) = \mu</math>, where <math>\phi(z):= \frac{z^2}{2}</math> and where <math>\xi</math> is a Brownian motion (specifically, <math>\xi=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}_t,\xi_t,\textbf{P}_x)</math> where <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F})</math> is a [[measurable space]], <math>(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> is a [[Filtration (probability theory)|filtration]], and <math>\xi_t</math> under <math>\textbf{P}_x</math> has the law of a Brownian motion started at <math>x</math>).

As will be clarified in the next section, <math>\phi</math> encodes an underlying branching mechanism, and <math>\xi</math> encodes the motion of the particles. Here, since <math>\xi</math> is a Brownian motion, the resulting object is known as a '''''Super-brownian motion'''''.<ref name=":0" />

=== Generalization to (ξ, ϕ)-superprocesses ===
Our discrete branching system <math>Y^N(t,dx)</math> can be much more sophisticated, leading to a variety of superprocesses:

* Instead of <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, the state space can now be any [[Polish space#Lusin spaces|Lusin space]] <math>E</math>.
* The underlying motion of the particles can now be given by <math>\xi=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}_t,\xi_t,\textbf{P}_x)</math>, where <math>\xi_t</math> is a [[càdlàg]] [[Markov process]] (see,<ref name=":0" /> Chapter 4, for details).
* A particle dies at rate <math>\gamma_N</math>
* When a particle dies at time <math>t</math>, located in <math>\xi_t</math>, it gives birth to a random number of offspring <math>n_{t,\xi_t}</math>. These offspring start to move from <math>\xi_t</math>. We require that the law of <math>n_{t,x}</math> depends solely on <math>x</math>, and that all <math>(n_{t,x})_{t,x}</math> are independent. Set <math>p_k(x)=\mathbb{P}[n_{t,x}=k]</math> and define <math>g</math> the associated [[probability-generating function]]:<math display="inline">g(x,z):=\sum\limits_{k=0}^\infty p_k(x)z^k</math>
Add the following requirement that the expected number of offspring is bounded:<math display="block">\sup\limits_{x\in E}\mathbb{E}[n_{t,x}]<+\infty</math>Define <math>X^N(t,dx):=\frac{1}{N}Y^N(t,dx)</math> as above, and define the following crucial function:<math display="block">\phi_N(x,z):=N\gamma_N \left[g_N\Big(x,1-\frac{z}{N}\Big)\,-\,\Big(1-\frac{z}{N}\Big)\right]</math>Add the requirement, for all <math>a\geq 0</math>, that <math>\phi_N(x,z)</math> is [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz continuous]] with respect to <math>z</math> uniformly on <math>E\times [0,a]</math>, and that <math>\phi_N</math> converges to some function <math>\phi</math> as <math>N\to +\infty</math> uniformly on <math>E\times [0,a]</math>.

Provided all of these conditions, the finite-dimensional distributions of <math>X^N(t)</math> converge to those of a measure-valued random process <math>X(t,dx)</math> which is called a <math>(\xi,\phi)</math>-'''''superprocess''''',<ref name=":0" /> with initial value <math>X(0) = \mu</math>.

==== Commentary on ϕ ====
Provided <math>\lim_{N\to+\infty}\gamma_N = +\infty</math>, that is, the number of branching events becomes infinite, the requirement that <math>\phi_N</math> converges implies that, taking a Taylor expansion of <math>g_N</math>, the expected number of offspring is close to 1, and therefore that the process is near-critical.

=== Generalization to Dawson-Watanabe superprocesses ===
The branching particle system <math>Y^N(t,dx)</math> can be further generalized as follows:

* The probability of death in the time interval <math>[r,t)</math> of a particle following trajectory <math>(\xi_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> is <math>\exp\left\{-\int_r^t\alpha_N(\xi_s)K(ds)\right\}</math> where <math>\alpha_N</math> is a positive measurable function and <math>K</math> is a continuous functional of <math>\xi</math> (see,<ref name=":0" /> chapter 2, for details).
* When a particle following trajectory <math>\xi</math> dies at time <math>t</math>, it gives birth to offspring according to a measure-valued [[probability kernel]] <math>F_N(\xi_{t-},d\nu)</math>. In other words, the offspring are not necessarily born on their parent's location. The number of offspring is given by <math>\nu(1)</math>. Assume that <math>\sup\limits_{x\in E}\int \nu(1)F_N(x,d\nu)<+\infty</math>.

Then, under suitable hypotheses, the finite-dimensional distributions of <math>X^N(t)</math> converge to those of a measure-valued random process <math>X(t,dx)</math> which is called a '''''Dawson-Watanabe''''' '''''superprocess''''',<ref name=":0" /> with initial value <math>X(0) = \mu</math>.

== Properties ==
A superprocess has a number of properties. It is a [[Markov process]], and its [[Markov kernel]] <math>Q_t(\mu,d\nu)</math> verifies the '''branching property''':<math display="block">Q_t(\mu+\mu',\cdot) = Q_t(\mu,\cdot)*Q_t(\mu',\cdot)</math>where <math>*</math> is the [[convolution]].A special class of superprocesses are '''<math> (\alpha,d,\beta)</math>-superprocesses''',<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Etheridge |first=Alison |title=An introduction to superprocesses |date=2000 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=0-8218-2706-5 |location=Providence, RI |oclc=44270365}}</ref> with <math> \alpha\in (0,2],d\in \N,\beta \in (0,1]</math>. A '''<math> (\alpha,d,\beta)</math>-superprocesses''' is defined on <math> \R^d</math>. Its ''branching mechanism'' is defined by its [[factorial moment generating function]] (the definition of a branching mechanism varies slightly among authors, some<ref name=":0" /> use the definition of <math> \phi</math> in the previous section, others<ref name=":1" /> use the factorial moment generating function):
:<math> \Phi(s) = \frac{1}{1+\beta}(1-s)^{1+\beta}+s</math>
and the spatial motion of individual particles (noted <math> \xi</math> in the previous section) is given by the <math>\alpha</math>-symmetric [[Lévy process|stable process]] with [[Generator (mathematics)|infinitesimal generator]] <math>\Delta_{\alpha}</math>.

The <math>\alpha = 2</math> case means <math> \xi</math> is a standard [[Brownian motion]] and the <math>(2,d,1)</math>-superprocess is called the super-Brownian motion.

One of the most important properties of superprocesses is that they are intimately connected with certain nonlinear [[partial differential equation]]s. The simplest such equation is <math>\Delta u-u^2=0\ on\  \mathbb{R}^d.</math> When the spatial motion (migration) is a diffusion process, one talks about a superdiffusion. The connection between superdiffusions  and nonlinear PDE's is similar to the one between diffusions and linear PDE's.
